# A. Multipoint Evaluation

## How to find it

Organize all moduli `x-X_i` in a product tree and propagate remainders.

## Correctness

Remainder transitivity makes each child remainder congruent to the original polynomial modulo its subtree product; at a leaf its constant is exactly the requested value.

## Complexity

`O(M(n+q) log q)` time and `O((n+q) log q)` aggregate polynomial storage.

At each node store `P mod product[node]`; since a child product divides its
parent product, reducing the parent's remainder again is equivalent to
reducing the original polynomial. Repeated points are legal and simply create
equal linear factors at different leaves.

# B. Polynomial Interpolation

## How to find it

Evaluate the derivative of the root product, form Lagrange weights, and merge them upward.

## Correctness

The root expansion is the Lagrange formula. It matches every sample value and has degree below `n`, so uniqueness proves equality.

## Complexity

`O(M(n) log n)` time.

The points must be distinct so that every `M'(X_i)` is invertible. Preserve
the association between each point and ordinate even if the tree is padded or
balanced internally.

# C. XOR Convolution

## How to find it

Use Walsh--Hadamard butterflies because XOR is addition in the vector space of bits.

## Correctness

Each Walsh character turns XOR into multiplication; inversion restores coefficients after pointwise products.

## Complexity

`O(k 2^k)` time and `O(2^k)` storage.

The forward and inverse butterflies have the same additions and subtractions;
only the inverse multiplies all entries by `inverse(2^k)`. A direct double
loop over pairs of masks is the ideal small oracle.

# D. Subset Convolution

## How to find it

Separate values by popcount, zeta-transform every rank, convolve ranks, then Möbius-invert.

## Correctness

Rank equality removes overlapping pairs: if ranks add to `|S|` and both sets lie in `S`, their union is `S` exactly when they are disjoint.

## Complexity

`O(k squared 2^k)` time and `O(k 2^k)` storage.

After zeta transformation, convolve the popcount ranks at each mask. Möbius
inversion must be applied rank by rank before selecting rank `|S|`; omitting
the ranks computes a different convolution that includes overlapping pairs.

# Distinguishing the tools

Use a product tree when many unrelated scalar evaluation moduli share one
polynomial. Use Walsh butterflies for XOR, subset-zeta for OR, supermask-zeta
for AND, and ranked subset-zeta for disjoint union. Stress each implementation
against its literal defining sum on dimensions up to five; this catches a
reversed loop direction more reliably than large samples.
